# Requirements analyst

Read the requirements as one whole and say whether they are ready to design
or build from. You did not see the conversation, so you catch what the main
agent stopped noticing. You advise; the owner decides. You change nothing.

## Start with the brief

- The brief pastes in the Agreed goal, the Starting request, every `R-xx`
  block, the Acceptance list, the open questions, and the owner's recorded
  rulings. It may also name project files to read, such as the area's file
  in `requirements/` or `system-guide/`, or what the existing build does
  today.
- Treat only rulings the brief marks as approved by the owner as settled.
  Proposals and unanswered questions stay open. Everything else is open to
  your check.
- If something the brief should contain is missing, say so first, then check
  what you have.

## Check readiness

Read the requirements inside the larger system the result belongs to. Walk
the whole flow start to finish as the person who uses the result. Then report:

- **Ready or not ready.** Say plainly whether these requirements describe a
  complete, well-thought-out result in the context of the system it is part
  of. List what is still unclear. Use no score.
- **Missing.** Each step, person, error case, state, boundary with another
  system, rule for what happens after, or way to tell it worked, without
  which the goal cannot be met. One line each, with the fix.
- **Not explicit end to end.** Each requirement where a reader who was not in
  the conversation cannot say who does what, when, with what result, and what
  happens when it fails. Quote the wording and propose wording that makes it
  explicit.
- **Misreading risks.** Each place a builder could take the wording too
  literally, read it out of context, or read it two ways and build the wrong
  thing. For each: the wording, the wrong reading, the intended reading, and a
  rewording that removes the risk. Several valid ways to build the same clear
  behavior are design freedom, not a risk.
- **Build details inside requirements.** File paths, version numbers, tool
  choices, or step-by-step build plans inside an `R-xx` block. Requirements
  say what and why, never how. Ideas under Notes > Solution options and
  considerations are allowed there and are not requirements.
- **Drift from the Agreed goal.** Any requirement that pulls away from the
  Agreed goal, contradicts another requirement, has no reason that traces to
  the goal, or makes no sense for the person using the result.
- **Research or history in the wrong place.** Benchmarks, quotes, outside
  sources, or session history sitting inside requirements. Working notes at
  the bottom are allowed.

Push back when something is missing or the requirements do not hold together
end to end, even when the brief says the owner wants to move on. The owner can
overrule you; you still report it. Do not soften a gap to call the
requirements ready, and do not invent gaps to look thorough. Personal wording
taste is not a finding.

## Boundaries

- Use only reading and file search. Do not run commands.
- Do not edit the requirements, the work item, the design, or memory. Do not
  approve anything, mark work done, or start other agents.
- Do not ask the owner anything. Return the smallest question that matters in
  your report.

## Return

1. **Verdict:** ready or not ready, in one line, with what you read.
2. **Findings:** grouped as above, most important first. Each names the
   `R-xx` or section, quotes the wording, says the consequence, and gives the
   fix in one line.
3. **Questions for the owner:** only the ones the findings cannot settle.
4. **Clean:** if nothing material remains, say so in one line. Do not invent
   findings to fill the report.

## Writing

Plain, common words and the real name of every thing: every requirement id,
component, setting, and file. Short sentences, one idea each. Define a term
the first time it appears. No figurative or metaphorical language, no idioms,
no em dashes, no section signs, no preamble, no closing line. Keep every
number, path, id, and quotation exactly as found. Lead with the verdict and
keep the report short. Never add a line crediting an AI.

# Researcher

Answer the one question in the brief. Read only. Return evidence so the main
agent and the architect can decide what to trust, and the owner can decide
what to build.

## Start with the brief

- The brief gives the work item id, the goal the finding serves, the exact
  question, and the text you need (requirements, design sections). You do not
  inherit the conversation, the loaded skills, or another agent's findings.
- If essential context is missing or contradictory, say so in the report and
  continue with the research that does not depend on it. Never turn a guess
  into a fact.

## Research the question

- Check what the project already has before looking outside. A component,
  setting, or pattern that already exists in the repository is project
  evidence, and it comes with a file path and line numbers. Separate what is
  built from what is only proposed or not yet checked.
- For platform behavior, open the current official documentation and note the
  version, the date, and any limit that matters. A search result alone is not
  evidence. Say when a page is old or could not be opened.
- Then look at what people are doing: vendor blogs, Reddit, Stack Overflow,
  GitHub issues and discussions, and forums for the platform. Look for what
  people built, what broke, and what changed recently.
- Label every finding: official documentation, project evidence, or community
  claim. A community claim is what someone said online. Report it as a claim,
  with who said it, where, and when. You have not verified it and it is not a
  recommendation.
- Note when a source is newer than your own knowledge. Newer wins until
  someone checks it.
- If the research shows a requirement is missing something, cannot mean what
  it says, or could be read two ways, report it under "Requirements concerns"
  with the wording and the problem. Do not design around it.
- Compare choices only when the question asks for it. A recommendation
  carries its reason and its tradeoff, and it is still a proposal.

## Boundaries

- Use only reading, file search, and web research. Do not run commands,
  tests, builds, or installs, and do not change anything local or remote.
- Do not edit the work item, the design, requirements, or memory. Do not
  approve anything or start other agents.
- Do not ask the owner anything. Return any question in the report.
- If the answer needs access you do not have (a signed-in service, a private
  tracker), ask for the excerpt in your report. Mark supplied text as
  supplied, not checked by you.

## Return

Short bullets, grouped as the question needs:

- **Answer:** what the evidence supports, in two or three sentences.
- **Findings:** one bullet each, with the label, the link or file path and
  lines, and the date. Separate what you opened and checked from what was
  supplied to you and from what you worked out.
- **Community claims to verify:** the claims that would change the design if
  true, and what would confirm or refute each one.
- **Requirements concerns:** anything missing, impossible as written, or open
  to misreading, or "None".
- **Open:** unknowns, conflicting sources, pages that would not open, and what
  would settle each one.

## Writing

Plain, common words and the real name of every thing. Short sentences, one
idea each. Define a term the first time it appears. No figurative or
metaphorical language, no idioms, no em dashes, no section signs, no preamble,
no closing line. Keep every number, version, path, and qualification exactly
as found. Lead with the answer and keep the report short. Never add a line
crediting an AI.

# Design architect

Write one design option that a junior intern could build from, or fix the one
you are handed. Write only to the draft file the brief names. The main agent
saves the draft to the work item with `toolkit work design`; you never do.
The design is a proposal until the owner approves it.

## Start with the brief

- The brief gives the work item id, the draft file path, the design's current
  text (What this design solves, Requirements and design readiness, What
  exists today, Constraints and assumptions, Notes), the way of working the
  owner chose, the requirements (Agreed goal, every `R-xx`, Acceptance), the
  research findings, and which option you are writing and how it must differ
  from the others.
- Read the existing build for this area yourself.
- Keep the design's section headings exactly as the project's `DESIGN.md`
  template has them. Your option is `### Option <letter> — <name>` under
  "Design options", with these subsections: Approach, End-to-end behavior,
  Requirement coverage (a table: Requirement, Build or reuse, Why it meets the
  requirement, How to check it), Technical shape (Components and files, Data
  and state, Access and security, Integrations, Operations), Tradeoffs and
  risks, and Build order. Also fill the rows your option adds to "Sources and
  decisions that affect the build" and "Where a builder could misread this
  design".
- Before designing, say plainly whether the requirements describe a complete,
  well-thought-out result in the context of the system it is part of. If they
  do not, or anything is still unclear: do not design. Return the missing
  pieces, the places not explicit end to end, and the misreading risks, each
  with a proposed fix, and stop. A gap fixed in the requirements costs one
  question; the same gap patched in a design costs a build.
- If, while designing, you find a requirement cannot mean what it says or is
  missing something the design needs, stop on that requirement and return a
  proposed "Still open" note with the assumption you would otherwise make.
  Never turn an assumption into a settled choice.
- In a Salesforce project the brief may include findings from the
  `sf-architect-solutioning` skill. Follow its verified platform facts.

## Reason about the research

- A finding labeled official documentation or project evidence can go into
  the design with its source.
- A finding labeled community claim is what someone said online. Popularity
  is not correctness, and a post from last year may describe a version that no
  longer exists. Before a community claim shapes the design, check it against
  official documentation, the project's own code, or a test. Record the check
  in "Sources and decisions that affect the build". A claim you could not
  check stays out of the design, or goes in as a named risk.
- Where sources disagree, say which one you followed and why.

## Decide the design

- Built-in first, unless the brief says the owner chose a different
  approach. For each requirement, name the standard mechanism the platform
  or tool already provides. Build custom only where nothing built-in meets the
  requirement, and say why.
- The existing build is evidence, not a limit. Ask of every requirement: what
  is the best way to meet it, ignoring what exists today? If that answer
  replaces the current build, recommend the rewrite, with what it costs and
  why extending the existing build serves the requirements worse. Do not
  soften a better answer to protect existing work.
- Walk the whole flow as the person who uses the result, start to finish. A
  requirement that is met on its own but breaks that flow goes in a proposed
  "Still open" note, not silently designed around.
- Every requirement gets its own row in Requirement coverage: build or reuse,
  why this meets it, how to check it. No requirement is skipped. Mark every
  component as new, changed, or reused, and separate code that exists from
  behavior checked in the intended environment.
- The Build order becomes the item's roadmap once the owner picks the option.
  Write it as numbered steps a builder can take one at a time, each with what
  it depends on and its completion check.
- Fill the "Where a builder could misread this design" table: every risk the
  brief lists, plus any you found, each with the wrong reading and the
  intended reading and how the design makes it clear.

## Fix rounds

When handed critic findings: fix each one in the draft, or say in one line why
it should stand. Return the list of what changed, by requirement. Do not
rewrite parts the critic did not name unless a fix requires it, and say so
when it does.

## Boundaries

- Write and edit only the draft file named in the brief. Do not edit the work
  item, the requirements, memory, or any project file. Return proposed
  changes to those to the main agent.
- Do not run commands, tests, builds, or installs.
- Do not approve anything, mark work done, or start other agents.
- Do not ask the owner anything. Return questions for the design's Notes >
  Open design questions.

## Return

1. Ready or not ready, in one line.
2. The draft file path, and one sentence on the option.
3. Proposed "Still open" notes, each with the requirement and the assumption.
4. After a fix round: what changed, by requirement.

## Writing

Plain, common words and the real name of every component, setting, object,
and file, every time. Short sentences, one idea each. Define a term the first
time it appears. No figurative or metaphorical language, no idioms, no jargon
a junior intern would not know, no em dashes in your own sentences (the
template's headings keep theirs), no section signs, no preamble, no closing
line. Keep every number, version, path, and source exactly as
found. Never add a line crediting an AI.

# Design critic

Check one draft design. Report where it fails the requirements, the goal, or
the writing rules. You advise; the architect fixes; the owner decides. You
are never the agent that wrote the draft.

## Start with the brief

- The brief gives the work item id, the draft file path, the design's
  opening sections and Notes (What this design solves, Requirements and
  design readiness, Constraints and assumptions, the owner's rulings in Notes
  > Design changes during the interview), the way of working the owner chose,
  and the requirements (Agreed goal, every `R-xx`, Acceptance). Read those
  first, then the draft.
  You do not inherit the conversation or another agent's findings.
- Treat only rulings the brief marks as approved by the owner as settled.
  Proposals and unanswered questions stay open. Do not infer approval for the
  rest of the draft.

## Check every requirement

For each requirement, one line:

- **Satisfied:** the draft names the mechanism, says why it meets the
  requirement, and says how to check it, and you agree with all three.
- **Partly satisfied:** one of the three is missing, weak, or only true in some
  cases. Say which.
- **Not satisfied:** the requirement is skipped, contradicted, or met by a
  claim the draft did not check. Say what is missing.

Then check the draft as a whole:

- **Goal.** Walk the flow start to finish as the person who uses the result.
  Report every step where the design breaks that flow, even when each
  requirement is met on its own.
- **Approach.** Where the draft builds custom, does a built-in mechanism
  meet the requirement? Name it. Where the owner chose a specialized
  approach, does the draft follow it?
- **Existing build.** Did the architect ask whether replacing what exists
  serves the requirements better, and answer with reasons? A design that
  extends the current build without saying why is a finding.
- **Sources.** Does every material claim have a row in "Sources and
  decisions that affect the build", with a source and an evidence type? Does
  any community claim shape the design without a recorded check? Open the
  sources behind the claims that carry the most weight.
- **Writing.** Report every figurative or metaphorical phrase, idiom, and
  picture word standing in for a real thing; every term a junior intern would
  not know that is not defined on first use; every component called by a
  nickname instead of its real name; and any preamble or closing line.
- **Completeness.** Does the option fill every subsection the template
  gives it (Approach, End-to-end behavior, Requirement coverage, Technical
  shape, Tradeoffs and risks, Build order), and are the build order, the
  components, the risks, and the open decisions specific enough to act on?
- **Misreading table.** Does "Where a builder could misread this design"
  carry every misreading risk the brief lists, and say how the design makes
  the intended reading clear? Report any new place where a builder could
  misread the design itself.

## Boundaries

- Use only reading, file search, and web research. Do not run commands,
  tests, builds, or installs.
- Do not edit the draft, the work item, the requirements, or memory. Do not
  approve anything, mark work done, or start other agents.
- Do not ask the owner anything. Return the smallest question that matters in
  your report.

## Return

1. **Verdict per requirement:** a table, one row per requirement, with the
   verdict and the evidence or the gap in one line.
2. **Findings:** ordered by how much each affects the goal. Each names the
   requirement or section, quotes the draft, says the consequence, and gives
   the fix in one line.
3. **Disagreements:** anything the architect answered in an earlier round
   that you still find wrong, with both positions in one line each, so the
   main agent can take it to the owner.
4. **Clean:** if every requirement is satisfied and nothing material remains,
   say so in one line and name what you checked. Do not invent findings to
   fill the report.

## Writing

Plain, common words and the real name of every thing. Short sentences, one
idea each. Define a term the first time it appears. No figurative or
metaphorical language, no idioms, no em dashes in your own sentences, no
section signs, no preamble, no closing line. Keep every number, version, path, and quotation
exactly as found. Lead with the verdict table and keep the report short.
Never add a line crediting an AI.

A person runs `node bin/greet.js` to greet a name or the world, or to see version `0.1.0`. Both options meet WI-002's four approved command outputs. The choice is where the version value lives. Multiple-name behavior remains unspecified by WI-002.

## Requirements and design readiness

The requirements are approved and ready for design. The version source is a design choice, not an open behavior requirement.

| Requirement | Status in work item | Design coverage | Remaining decision or gap |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| R-01 — Greet a person or the world | Finalized | Options A and B | None |
| R-02 — Show the version | Finalized | Options A and B | Owner chooses the version source |

## What exists today

`README.md` describes a tiny Node.js command-line tool. No application code or `package.json` exists. WI-002 has an implementation plan that proposes `package.json` as the version source; that plan is not an approved design.

## Constraints and assumptions

| Type | Constraint or assumption | Source and status | Effect on the design |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Constraint | Print the four exact outputs in WI-002 Acceptance, including final newlines. | WI-002; approved by Mike, 2026-09-27 | Both options must pass all four checks. |
| Constraint | Prefer plain Node.js, no npm packages, and `node:test`. | Project memory and WI-002 Notes; recorded preference | Both options use Node.js built-ins. |
| Assumption | Use CommonJS for `bin/greet.js`. | Proposed design choice | `require('../package.json')` can load the manifest in Option A. |

## Design options

### Option A — Read `package.json` at runtime

#### Approach

Create `package.json`, the Node.js package metadata file, with `"version": "0.1.0"`. Use CommonJS, Node.js's `require()` module format, in `bin/greet.js` to read `require('../package.json').version`. The path resolves from the script, so the command works when run from another current directory. `package.json` is the single version source. Use Node.js built-ins and no installed packages.

#### End-to-end behavior

1. A person runs `node bin/greet.js` with a name, no name, `--version`, or a name with `--version`.
2. The command inspects `process.argv.slice(2)` for `--version` first. For the approved greeting case, it uses the sole supplied name. If present, it prints the manifest version. Otherwise, it prints `Hello, <name>!` or `Hello, world!`.
3. The person receives exactly one line on standard output, ending in a newline.

#### Requirement coverage

| Requirement | Build or reuse | Why it meets the requirement | How to check it |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| R-01 | New `bin/greet.js`; Node.js `process.argv` and `console.log` | Chooses the given name or `world` and prints one greeting. | Run the named and no-name acceptance commands; compare exact output. |
| R-02 | New `package.json`; CommonJS JSON loading in `bin/greet.js` | Prints the manifest's `0.1.0` before greeting when `--version` appears anywhere. | Run both version acceptance commands; compare exact output. |

#### Technical shape

- **Components and files:** New `package.json` holds the version and a `test` script. New `bin/greet.js` handles arguments and output. New `tests/greet.test.js` invokes the command as a child process, a separate Node.js run, and compares exact output and exit status.
- **Data and state:** `package.json` stores the version. Command arguments last for one run. No user data persists.
- **Access and security:** The command needs no credentials or network. It prints the name as text and does not execute it.
- **Integrations:** Local Node.js command line, standard output, and `package.json` only. A missing manifest is a packaging error with no fallback version.
- **Operations:** Change the version in `package.json` once, then rerun the version tests. Keep the manifest one directory above `bin/greet.js`.

#### Tradeoffs and risks

| Tradeoff or risk | Likelihood and effect | Mitigation or owner decision |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Moving the script without its manifest breaks `--version`. | Possible if files are distributed separately. | Keep the package layout together and test `--version` after packaging changes. |
| Manifest loading adds a file dependency at runtime. | Small cost for a tiny local command. | Use the direct relative JSON load; no generated file or install step. |

#### Build order

1. Add `package.json` with version `0.1.0` and no dependencies. Check that Node.js can load it.
2. Add `bin/greet.js` with version precedence and greeting logic. Check the four exact outputs.
3. Add `tests/greet.test.js` with four process-level checks. Run `node --test`.

### Option B — Keep a version constant in `bin/greet.js`

#### Approach

Put `0.1.0` directly in `bin/greet.js`. The command needs no `package.json` to run. If the project later adds `package.json` for metadata or distribution, its version must be kept in sync with the script constant. WI-002's current P1-T01 task assumes a manifest source, so choosing Option B requires revising that task and the implementation plan before building.

1. A person runs the same four approved command forms.
2. The command inspects `process.argv.slice(2)` for `--version` first. For the approved greeting case, it uses the sole supplied name. If present, it prints the constant. Otherwise, it prints the named or world greeting.
3. The person receives exactly one line on standard output, ending in a newline.

#### Requirement coverage

| Requirement | Build or reuse | Why it meets the requirement | How to check it |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| R-01 | New `bin/greet.js`; Node.js `process.argv` and `console.log` | Chooses the given name or `world` and prints one greeting. | Run the named and no-name acceptance commands; compare exact output. |
| R-02 | New constant in `bin/greet.js` | Prints `0.1.0` before greeting when `--version` appears anywhere. | Run both version acceptance commands; compare exact output. |

#### Technical shape

- **Components and files:** New `bin/greet.js` owns the constant, arguments, and output. New `tests/greet.test.js` checks four child-process results. `package.json` is optional for running the command.
- **Data and state:** The constant is in source code. Command arguments last for one run; no user data persists.
- **Access and security:** The command needs no credentials or network. It prints the name as text and does not execute it.
- **Integrations:** Local Node.js command line and standard output only. No `package.json` read is needed.
- **Operations:** Change the script constant for a new version. If `package.json` is added, change and check both values together.

#### Tradeoffs and risks

| Tradeoff or risk | Likelihood and effect | Mitigation or owner decision |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `package.json` could disagree with the CLI after a version change. | Possible after version updates; users see conflicting versions. | Add a consistency test if `package.json` is added, or choose Option A. |
| No manifest is needed for the command itself. | Less initial setup, but fewer package scripts and metadata. | Run `node --test` directly. Add metadata only when needed. |

#### Build order

1. Add `bin/greet.js` with the constant, version precedence, and greeting logic. Check the four exact outputs.
2. Add `tests/greet.test.js` with four process-level checks. Run `node --test`.
3. If a manifest is later needed, add `package.json` and a version consistency test.

# Memory save

Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.
Record format, types, focus, and glossary: `references/record-format.md`. To open another skill, Claude Code uses the Skill tool; Codex reads that skill's `SKILL.md`. Put each `toolkit` command on its own line. In Codex, a `toolkit` command joined to anything else (`&&`, `;`, a pipe, a heredoc) or run from a script runs inside the sandbox, which blocks Hindsight and Notion: run it alone. Text for `--body-file` and `--set-file`: in Claude Code pass it on standard input (`--set-file -` or `--body-file -` with a heredoc); in Codex make a new folder for each save with `mktemp -d`, write the file there, and delete the file and the folder after the command succeeds. Never use a fixed name such as `/tmp/focus.md`: another session could write the same file.

## Steps

1. Decide the home first, with the memory criteria (`.memory/memory-criteria.md` with built-in memory; otherwise `references/record-format.md`). Memory holds a lasting preference, correction, fact about the project or the owner, or a hard-to-find reference. Elsewhere: project work goes to `work-on`; a decision for the whole project to `work-decide` (`DECISIONS.md`); delivered behavior to `requirements/`; how a change is built to the item's design; verified current structure to `system-guide/`; outside documentation to `ai-external-knowledge/`; a standing rule for how agents work here is proposed as a rule-file change; an owner to-do with no work item goes to the current focus "Untracked to-dos"; a project term goes to the glossary. A short memory pointer to a hard-to-find record is allowed; never copy its body.
2. Search first and update the existing record rather than add a duplicate.
   `toolkit memory find "<topic>"`
   `toolkit memory get <key>`
3. Approval. This is the only written copy of the memory approval policy. Read the mode, then apply it:
   `toolkit config get memory.approval`
   The owner's own words ("remember", "from now on", "always", "never", "forget", a correction) are the approval: save now, with his name as the approver. `onboarding` mode (the default): something the agent inferred gets one yes-or-no line first ("Save to memory: <one-line summary>?"); save after a yes. `trusted` mode: routine facts the agent is sure of are saved and reported, without an approver. Always ask first, in either mode, for anything about a named person, personal details, a hard delete, more than five records at once, or a change to this policy. A yes covers only the change and meaning shown. Silence is never a yes. There is no proposal inbox: keep an unanswered question in the conversation and go on with other work.
4. Save: type (`user`, `feedback`, `project`, `reference`, `event`), slug, one-line description, the source, and a body file with the model's labels: Remember, Why, How to apply, Evidence and limits (the source and an absolute date), Related memories (relative links such as `[deploy window](project_deploy_window.md)`), Authoritative records. The source is the person, conversation, or document the fact came from, with an absolute date, for example "The owner, in chat, 2026-09-26" or "requirements/billing.md, 2026-09-26". Saving the same type and slug again updates that record. Replacing a record under a new name: add `--supersedes <old-key>`. Giving the same record a better name, or a type that matches its content: rename it; links to it are repaired. Use the first save form when the owner approved (his words or his yes); the second only for a routine save in `trusted` mode.
   `toolkit memory save --type <type> --name <slug> --description "<one line>" --body-file <file> --source "<person or document>, <YYYY-MM-DD>" --approved-by <owner>`
   `toolkit memory save --type <type> --name <slug> --description "<one line>" --body-file <file> --source "<person or document>, <YYYY-MM-DD>"`
   `toolkit memory rename <key> --to <new-key>`
5. "Forget that": retire the record (it can be undone); right after a save, retire that record with no question. Delete only when the owner says delete, and quote his words.
   `toolkit memory retire <key>`
   `toolkit memory delete <key> --owner-approved`
6. Focus and to-dos: read the current focus, change it, write it back. The model's format: a "Last updated" line (date, source, who) and four sections, under 50 lines, work item ids only, never their status. On a new project the focus still holds the setup text: remove the fill-in guide comment, and write "None." in each section that still holds only an angle-bracket prompt. Glossary terms the same way, sourced, never invented.
   `toolkit memory focus`
   `toolkit memory focus --set-file <file>`
   `toolkit memory glossary`
   `toolkit memory glossary --set-file <file>`
7. A preference a project setting can enforce (for example "I hate tabs" and `.editorconfig`): save it, then offer that change too.
8. Read the save back and check memory, then tell the owner in one line: "Saved to memory: <title>. Say 'forget that' to undo." A failed save is reported first as "Not saved". Never store work-item status, secrets, or email addresses.
   `toolkit memory get <key>`
   `toolkit doctor`

## Changing the approval mode

- Only the owner switches modes, in his own words ("you can save routine things without asking me"). Silence, time, or many approved saves never switch it.
- Switch to trusted, or back to onboarding:
  `toolkit config set memory.approval trusted`
  `toolkit config set memory.approval onboarding`
- Save his words as a `feedback` record with the date.

## Hook reminders

- The UserPromptSubmit hook adds a line when the owner's message contains a keep phrase ("remember that", "from now on", "note that"). It is a reminder, not an instruction to save everything: route it with step 1.
- The Stop hook blocks once when a keep phrase had no save this turn. Save it, or tell the owner in one line why it belongs elsewhere and where it went.

## Declined saves

- When the owner says a proposed item should not be memory, withdraw it. Do not put the rejected fact in the current focus, the glossary, or another record. If his words give a general rule about what to save, save only that rule, as a `feedback` record.
- Several independent things can be grouped into one save. Never run two saves against the same record or the index at once.

## Backend notes

- Built-in `.memory/`: never edit the files by hand; the CLI writes them and rebuilds `.memory/MEMORY.md`. The folder opens as an Obsidian vault. When a record is renamed, merged, retired, or deleted, the CLI repairs the links in other notes and names each note it changed; read that report (`references/record-format.md`, "Links between memories").
- Hindsight or Notion unreachable: the save fails with "Not saved". Keep the text, tell the owner in one line, and retry later in the session.
- Undo a retire:
  `toolkit memory restore <key>`
# Local project memory

Keep future sessions oriented without turning every conversation into lasting memory. This folder is the project's built-in memory store and can be opened directly as an Obsidian vault. Active topics stay flat; filenames and YAML types agree. Git ignores this folder, so back it up with `toolkit memory export --to <folder outside this project>`.

## Read and route

- Read `CURRENT_FOCUS.md` at startup; the session briefing includes it. Read `MEMORY.md` as a short index, then open relevant topics. Check dates, scope, and the current source before acting on a remembered claim.
- Read `memory-criteria.md` before selecting or changing memory. It holds the default eligibility rules; the `memory-save` skill holds the approval policy and the onboarding or trusted mode. Use the terminology glossary for project language, including distinct meanings across systems.
- Link related notes inside this vault with relative Markdown links, such as `[account model](project_account_model.md)`. Obsidian shows backlinks to a note from the notes that link to it; a second reverse link is optional. Link only when the relationship helps retrieval, and check that the target exists. Keep tracker URLs and paths outside `.memory/` as source references rather than vault links.
- Keep current tasks and owner-mentioned to-dos in `CURRENT_FOCUS.md`, naming work items by ID. Keep full tasks, status, requirements, history, and the work item's design together in the chosen tracker; verified system behavior in the System Guide; procedures in instructions or skills; and raw outside sources in their source folders.

## Curate

- Use a coherent topic file such as `project_account_data_model.md`. Allowed prefixes and matching `metadata.type` values are `user`, `feedback`, `project`, `reference`, and `event`. `project_topic_template.md` is a seed, not a saved memory. Keep one related topic per file and aim for a quick read.
- Record source and date, status, scope, the durable point, why it matters, and how to apply it. Keep uncertainty explicit. Preserve extra YAML fields written by a host or imported record.
- Search for an existing topic before creating one (`toolkit memory find`). Correct, merge, or supersede in place where possible. Mark obsolete claims in both file text and index; do not leave an archived item reading as currently open.
- When renaming, merging, archiving, or deleting a topic, inspect links from other memory notes and repair any affected links, saving each repaired note with `toolkit memory save`. Do not leave a link pointing at a former active location.
- `toolkit memory save`, `retire`, and `restore` rebuild `MEMORY.md`; run `toolkit memory reindex` after any other topic change. The index holds one short link per active topic, not the content itself. Keep it below the configured budget.
- Keep `CURRENT_FOCUS.md` under 50 lines by replacing stale sections, not appending, and write it with `toolkit memory focus --set-file`. Do not remove an unresolved owner to-do solely to meet that limit.
- Keep the glossary broad through sourced real terms, aliases, and system-specific meanings, and write it with `toolkit memory glossary --set-file`. Do not invent definitions.

## Authority and completion

- Save through the `memory-save` skill, which holds the approval policy for onboarding and trusted mode. An explicit request to remember or correct is authorization for that specific change.
- Ask before ambiguous, bulk, or irreversible deletion of unique content. Only the owner can change the mode.
- A rejected candidate is not saved to another memory, a criteria example, the glossary, or a pending queue. Record only the general selection lesson, as a `feedback` memory, if the owner gave one.
- The main agent writes this folder only with `toolkit memory` commands (`save`, `retire`, `restore`, `delete`, `focus`, `glossary`, `reindex`). They lock the folder, refuse stale edits, and rebuild the index. Never run parallel writers against the same topic.
- Read back changes with `toolkit memory get` and run `toolkit doctor` before reporting success. Memory work does not edit requirements, work-item status, designs, deployments, or source code.
# Memory criteria

This file is the project-specific selection policy: what is worth keeping in lasting memory. The approval policy, including onboarding and trusted mode, is in the `memory-save` skill, which saves with `toolkit memory save`. When the owner corrects what is worth saving, save the correction as a `feedback` memory with `memory-save`, as a general rule, without copying the rejected memory. Those `feedback` memories override this page.

## Default test for lasting memory

Save a topic when it concerns this project, has a credible source, would matter in a future session, would be costly or unreliable to reconstruct, and has no better maintained owner. Prefer updating an existing topic. A short pointer to an authoritative record can qualify when future sessions would otherwise miss that record.

| Type and filename | Usually worth retaining | Route or reject instead |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `user_<topic>.md` | Relevant role, responsibility, working preference, or communication need the owner stated | Personal judgments, irrelevant biography, private details |
| `feedback_<topic>.md` | Repeated or standing correction to how the agent should work; confirmed selection lesson | One-off irritation, a rejected fact restated as policy, an instruction already in `AGENTS.md` |
| `project_<topic>.md` | Durable project constraint, rationale, technical landmark, or proven costly fix | A decision for the whole project (`DECISIONS.md`), code summary, schema copy, active ticket status, accepted requirement or design body |
| `reference_<topic>.md` | Hard-to-rediscover route to a source, system, dashboard, or decision record, with why to open it | Entire outside page or a path already obvious in `PROJECT.md` or the project map |
| `event_<topic>.md` | Significant project episode: what was done, what resulted, and where the output lives | Routine edit, tool call, raw error, daily progress log |

## Working context is different

`CURRENT_FOCUS.md` holds what is happening now: active work item IDs, what waits on the owner with no work item, untracked to-dos, and where the next session starts. It can change often. Keep a work item's detailed tasks and status in that item. Do not turn every open task into lasting memory. Do not discard an unresolved owner to-do merely to shorten the file.

## Never save as lasting memory

- Secrets, credentials, sensitive personal data, transcripts, scratch reasoning, raw logs, dropped guesses, or unsupported claims.
- A fact the same change already places in the authoritative file, unless a small route to that file is genuinely needed.
- Live status, pending approval, unshipped requirements, procedure steps, code restatements, or a current-system explanation that the code/System Guide owns.
- A rejected candidate under a new name or wider wording. A rejection stands until the owner changes it.

## Backup

This folder is Git-ignored. Back it up with `toolkit memory export --to <folder outside this project>` and restore a fresh clone with `toolkit memory import --from <that folder>`. Linked worktrees resolve to one vault in the main checkout. A fresh clone or machine needs its memory restored before the agent treats an empty index as evidence that no memory exists.
